families.description: High-volume RaaS known for fast encryption, affiliate autonomy and repeated leaks of its builder.
families.name: LockBit

families.description: RaaS that moved from Windows-only encryption to Linux and ESXi variants, with a Rust Megazord encryptor.
families.name: Akira

families.description: Data-theft-first operation best known for mass exploitation of managed file-transfer products.
families.name: Cl0p

families.description: Closed ransomware group with custom encryption and double extortion, active across government and enterprise.
families.name: Play

families.description: RaaS that absorbed affiliates from disrupted operations; no stable file extension is reliable for identification.
families.name: RansomHub

families.description: Rust-based RaaS associated with high-impact healthcare and critical-infrastructure intrusions.
families.name: ALPHV / BlackCat

families.description: RaaS with a long-lived leak site, broad targeting and repeated use of vulnerable internet-facing services.
families.name: Medusa

families.description: RaaS that combined email bombing and vishing with fast enterprise-wide encryption; activity declined after 2024.
families.name: Black Basta

families.description: RaaS known for healthcare and education intrusions and a short dwell time before encryption.
families.name: Rhysida

families.description: RaaS formerly tracked as Agenda, with cross-platform encryptors and high leak-site volume.
families.name: Qilin

families.description: Predecessor/related brand to BlackSuit, with partial encryption and service-stop techniques.
families.name: Royal

families.description: High-impact RaaS whose internal leaks exposed much of the affiliate playbook still reused today.
families.name: Conti

families.description: RaaS dismantled by law enforcement in 2023; its encryptors and affiliate playbook remain in use.
families.name: Hive

families.description: RaaS that popularised large-scale double extortion and supply-chain-style attacks.
families.name: REvil / Sodinokibi

families.description: Legacy big-game ransomware distributed through TrickBot and Emotet infrastructure.
families.name: Ryuk

families.description: Self-propagating worm that caused global disruption in 2017; still useful as a detection regression case.
families.name: WannaCry

families.description: Early mass-distribution encryptor that normalised ransomware delivery through malicious attachments.
families.name: Locky

families.description: Long-running family with many variants and a low-cost affiliate model aimed at smaller victims.
families.name: Phobos

families.description: RaaS focused on data theft and double extortion, often using Phobos-derived encryptors.
families.name: 8Base

families.description: Group that shifted toward data-only extortion while retaining encryptor capability.
families.name: BianLian

families.description: Successor brand to Royal, using partial encryption and service disruption.
families.name: BlackSuit

families.description: RaaS that uses double extortion and encrypts large virtualised estates.
families.name: Cactus

families.description: RaaS active against Windows, Linux and NAS systems, with a focus on smaller victims.
families.name: Chaos

families.description: Newer RaaS brand observed in 2025 with double extortion and ESXi support.
families.name: NightSpire

families.description: RaaS documented by CISA in 2025, using double extortion and data-theft pressure.
families.name: Interlock

families.description: High-volume 2026 RaaS; no stable extension is reliable, so detection is behavioural.
families.name: SafePay

families.description: RaaS that expanded in 2026, targeting government and critical infrastructure with double extortion.
families.name: Gunra

families.description: Long-running operation that exploits outdated internet-facing software and rotates encryptor variants.
families.name: Ghost (Cring)

families.description: Related/overlapping RaaS brands tracked together in 2026 reporting; extensions vary by affiliate.
families.name: INC / Lynx / Sinobi

families.description: RaaS that became one of the more active leak-site operations in 2026.
families.name: DragonForce

families.description: New RaaS brand with high 2026 leak-site volume and affiliate-driven targeting.
families.name: The Gentlemen

families.description: RaaS observed targeting virtualised environments and education.
families.name: Fog

families.description: Long-running group with data-leak extortion and a smaller encryption footprint.
families.name: Everest

families.description: Smaller RaaS brand with data-theft extortion and affiliate activity.
families.name: Kill Security

families.description: Data-theft extortion operation; may not deploy an encryptor, so file extensions are not a reliable signal.
families.name: World Leaks

families.description: RaaS with data-leak extortion; no stable extension is known.
families.name: Devman

families.description: Group linked to former Hive affiliates; uses generic .locked markers, so family attribution is weak from extension alone.
families.name: Hunters International

families.description: RaaS using a Rust-based cross-platform encryptor; overlaps with ALPHV affiliate tradecraft.
families.name: Cicada3301

families.description: Long-running family with frequent variants and vulnerable-service initial access.
families.name: Mallox

families.description: Commodity family with many variants and a low-complexity affiliate model.
families.name: Makop

families.description: RaaS with double extortion and a broad Windows/Linux target set.
families.name: Trigona

families.description: Smaller RaaS brand with double extortion and commodity initial access.
families.name: Abyss

families.description: Group known for high-value financial targets and exploitation of internet-facing appliances.
families.name: Cuba

families.description: Group known for manual intrusion and virtual-machine-aware encryption; disrupted in 2023.
families.name: Ragnar

families.description: RaaS that combined encryption with DDoS pressure; activity faded after 2021.
families.name: SunCrypt

families.description: Group focused on schools and hospitals, often using data theft and intermittent encryption.
families.name: Vice Society

families.description: RaaS with recurring variants and ESXi support, including a 2023 CISA advisory.
families.name: BlackByte

families.description: RaaS associated with Conti/Diavol affiliates and fast encryption.
families.name: Quantum

families.description: RaaS that shut down in 2021 and released decryption keys.
families.name: Avaddon

families.description: RaaS linked to Maze and Sekhmet, known for printing ransom notes on victim printers.
families.name: Egregor

families.description: Group that combined encryption with data-leak extortion and large-file targeting.
families.name: Nefilim

families.description: Group that popularised publishing stolen data when victims refused to pay.
families.name: Maze

families.description: Group disrupted in 2021; targeted healthcare and education during the pandemic.
families.name: NetWalker

families.description: RaaS that shut down after the Colonial Pipeline incident; predecessor to BlackMatter.
families.name: DarkSide

families.description: RaaS that succeeded DarkSide and was linked to ALPHV/BlackCat.
families.name: BlackMatter

families.description: Group that exploits internet-facing vulnerabilities and uses double extortion.
families.name: HelloKitty

families.description: RaaS successor to Cyclops, with cross-platform encryption and data theft.
families.name: Knight

families.description: Group known for exfiltration-first operations and use of legitimate remote-access tooling.
families.name: Lorenz

families.description: Ransomware that targets NAS shares, often with low-and-slow encryption across many extensions.
families.name: Checkmate

families.description: Cross-platform family known for Linux and ESXi variants and high-value targets.
families.name: RansomEXX

families.description: Linux-focused encryptor observed in 2023, with a smaller Windows footprint.
families.name: IceFire

families.description: Linux encryptor derived from an open-source project, useful as a lab and regression case.
families.name: Gonnacry

families.description: Early cross-platform family known for compromising Linux web servers.
families.name: Erebus

families.description: Family whose source leak seeded many ESXi encryptors still seen in later campaigns.
families.name: Babuk

families.description: Mass-exploitation campaign that encrypted ESXi datastores and left .args files.
families.name: ESXiArgs

families.description: Historical family that established the modern ransomware payment model.
families.name: CryptoLocker

families.description: Mass-distribution family from the exploit-kit era; useful for regression testing.
families.name: CryptoWall

families.description: Historical family that targeted gaming files and later released its keys.
families.name: TeslaCrypt

families.description: Early Tor-based locker; no single reliable extension across variants.
families.name: CTB-Locker

families.description: Destructive wiper disguised as ransomware; included because behaviour overlaps with encryption attacks.
families.name: NotPetya

families.description: Worm-like encryptor that spread through fake updates and network shares.
families.name: Bad Rabbit

families.description: High-volume RaaS that retired in 2019 after claiming large payouts.
families.name: GandCrab

families.description: BitPaymer-derived group active in big-game and healthcare incidents.
families.name: DoppelPaymer

families.description: RaaS known for remote-access tooling and affiliate support.
families.name: AvosLocker

families.description: RaaS that evolved into the Astro team and used data-leak extortion.
families.name: Mount Locker

families.description: Group linked to Wizard Spider tradecraft and big-game hunting.
families.name: Hades
